claims.text: Near-equiatomic, single-phase high-entropy alloys can contain local chemical order rather than behaving as ideal random solid solutions.
Increasing local chemical order makes the dislocation energy landscape more rugged.
Increasing local chemical order raises activation barriers for dislocation activity.
An equiatomic, single-phase HEA can be prepared with a nominally random solid-solution structure.
Controlled annealing promotes local chemical order in the proposed alloy.
Rapid quenching maintains a comparatively disordered elemental distribution in the proposed alloy.
Local chemical order produces spatial variations in generalized planar fault energies.
Local chemical order increases lattice friction through a nanoscale segment-detrapping mechanism.
The increased lattice friction impedes dislocation glide.
A high-LCO state will have greater yield strength than an otherwise identical chemically disordered state.
A high-LCO state will have greater hardness than an otherwise identical chemically disordered state.
Increasing local chemical order may reduce ductility.
The proposed LCO-controlled behavior is expected to hold below approximately 0.5 times the melting temperature.
The hypothesis applies only while the alloy remains single phase and local ordering does not generate secondary phases.
The hypothesis is limited to temperature and stress regimes in which dislocation glide is the dominant deformation mechanism.
Grain-boundary-related strengthening can confound attribution of strength changes to local chemical order.
The magnitude of hardness and strength changes depends on elemental makeup and processing history.
A lack of statistically significant strength and hardness increases, or a lack of correlation between measured LCO and mechanical performance, would falsify the proposed governing role of LCO.
